title: One Foot in Each Country: the Soldier, the Stove-Heated Room, and the Bones That Kept Travelling
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: La Haye en Touraine, the birth in the grandmother's house
stops.date_confidence: attested; the birth date is fixed by the baptismal register three days later
stops.campa: In his maternal grandmother's house at La Haye en Touraine a son is born to Joachim Descartes, councillor in the parlement of Brittany, and to Jeanne Brochard. The town has carried that name for centuries and will carry it two more. The father's court sits at Rennes, weeks of bad road away, and he is not present. The infant is small and coughs. He will live fifty-three years and arrange nearly all of them around a body he was told from the beginning could not be relied on. For now the household does not expect him to last the month.
suggested_refs: The maison natale at La Haye, now the Musée Descartes in the town centre
sources: A.C. Grayling, Descartes: The Life of René Descartes and Its Place in His Times (2005)
Geneviève Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Église Saint-Georges, the baptism
stops.date_confidence: attested; surviving parish register entry
stops.campa: Three days after the birth the child is carried into the parish church and christened René. The register names the father, Joachim Descartes, councillor in the parlement of Brittany, and it is that single entry on which every later account of the family's standing rests. The Descartes are lawyers and physicians, provincial gentry with arms and no great fortune. What will come to this third child is land in Poitou, farms and rents, the kind of inheritance a man is supposed to hold and pass on. He will sell all of it.
suggested_refs: The twelfth-century Église Saint-Georges de La Haye, remodelled in the fifteenth century, listed 1926
sources: Baptismal register of La Haye, cited in Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Châtellerault, the house of the grandmother
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mother's death (fr.wikipedia gives 13 May 1597); the years of fostering are reconstruction
stops.campa: Jeanne Brochard dies thirteen months after this son is born, in childbed with another infant who does not outlive her by much. The boy is handed to his grandmother Jeanne Sain and to a nurse at Châtellerault while his father remarries and keeps to Brittany for the parlement's sessions. He grows up among women and servants, pale, excused from the ordinary discipline of a small boy because he is thought too weak to bear it. The mornings in bed begin here. Nobody ever withdraws the exemption.
suggested_refs: The Brochard and Sain family property at Châtellerault, where the infant was fostered
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Collège Royal Henri-Le-Grand, La Flèche: eight years of the Jesuits
stops.date_confidence: sources differ: entry given as 1606 or Easter 1607, departure as 1614 or 1615; the Prytanée's own account says a pupil from 1607 to 1615
stops.campa: He boards at the Jesuit college Henri IV founded three years earlier by handing a royal château to the Society, among sons of the nobility, for eight years of Latin, rhetoric, logic, Aristotelian physics, and mathematics. His health earns him a standing dispensation: while the others go down to the first lessons he is allowed to stay in bed, and he reads there. Of everything taught in the place, only the mathematics will strike him as certain. Nobody, he decides, has yet built anything worth having on top of it. He leaves at nineteen.
stops.quote: I was studying in one of the most celebrated schools in Europe, in which I thought there must be learned men, if such were anywhere to be found.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part I, tr. John Veitch (1853); Descartes does not name La Flèche in the passage, the identification is standard biography
suggested_refs: The Collège Royal Henri-Le-Grand, later the Prytanée National Militaire, La Flèche
sources: Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part One (1637)
Stephen Gaukroger, Descartes: An Intellectual Biography (1995)

stops.name: University of Poitiers, the law degree he never uses
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the degree (SEP chronology); the day and month are not in the reachable record
stops.campa: At Poitiers he reads canon and civil law, takes the baccalaureate and then the licence, and acquires the qualification a magistrate's son is expected to carry. There is no bar to be admitted to and he joins no practice. The degree closes out the portion of his life that other people arranged for him. From here every move is his own. He leaves Poitiers with the licence in hand and nothing arranged to follow it, and where he spends the next months is not established.
stops.quote: As soon as my age permitted me to pass from under the control of my instructors, I entirely abandoned the study of letters, and resolved no longer to seek any other science than the knowledge of myself, or of the great book of the world.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part I, tr. John Veitch (1853), Project Gutenberg e-text 59
suggested_refs: The Faculty of Law at Poitiers, where the baccalauréat and licence were taken in 1616
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Paris, the Faubourg Saint-Germain
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Baillet's account of these Paris months, treated cautiously by later scholars
stops.campa: In Paris he keeps the company his rank puts in front of him: gamblers, fencers, young men with money and no employment. Baillet, writing forty years after his death, has him disappearing out of all that into lodgings in the Faubourg Saint-Germain to work at geometry with the mathematician Claude Mydorge, and being hunted down there by friends who had lost track of him. The story rests on Baillet alone. He is twenty-one. Within two years he has left France for a war.
suggested_refs: Adrien Baillet, La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes (1691), the earliest full biography
sources: Baillet, La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes (1691)

stops.name: Breda, enlisted as a gentleman volunteer
stops.date_confidence: attested year; month not fixed in the reachable sources
stops.campa: He crosses to the Dutch Republic and takes service at Breda under Maurice of Nassau as a gentleman volunteer, unpaid, in an army sitting out the last years of a twelve-year truce with Spain. The arrangement costs him nothing and commands him to nothing; it gives a young man with an income the freedom of Europe and a reason to be anywhere. He is twenty-two. He has no intention of a soldier's career and afterwards describes these years as reading rather than serving.
stops.quote: I spent the remainder of my youth in traveling, in visiting courts and armies, in holding intercourse with men of different dispositions and ranks, in collecting varied experience.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part I, tr. John Veitch (1853), Project Gutenberg e-text 59
suggested_refs: The garrison of the Dutch States Army at Breda under Maurice of Nassau

stops.name: Breda, the placard in the marketplace
stops.date_confidence: the meeting and the correspondence are attested to late 1618; the placard anecdote is traditional
stops.campa: A mathematical problem is posted in Dutch in the Breda marketplace, a public challenge of the sort the town's calculators set one another. Descartes has no Dutch and asks the man standing next to him to put it into French. The man is Isaac Beeckman, a physician's son from Middelburg who thinks about falling bodies, vibrating strings, and water pressed through tubes. Descartes brings him the solution. The placard comes down to us only through Baillet; the notebooks the two of them fill with mechanics over the following year are in their own hands.
suggested_refs: The Descartes-Beeckman correspondence and Beeckman's Journal, 1618-1619, in Adam and Tannery, Oeuvres de Descartes
sources: Adam and Tannery, eds., Oeuvres de Descartes
en.wikipedia, 'Isaac Beeckman' (which hedges the placard story explicitly)

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the crowning of the emperor
stops.date_confidence: attested for the coronation (elected 28 August, crowned 9 September 1619); the dossier's original 1619-07 was two months early
stops.campa: Ferdinand of Styria is elected in August and crowned at Frankfurt in September, in a city crowded with ambassadors and soldiers waiting to see which way Bohemia will go. Descartes travels there for it. From Frankfurt he takes service with Maximilian of Bavaria, on the Catholic side of a war that has just opened and will run thirty years. Inside a year he has worn the colours of both halves of Europe's confessional quarrel. Nothing he wrote names either side as his.
suggested_refs: The coronation of Ferdinand II at Frankfurt, 9 September 1619

stops.name: Neuburg an der Donau, the room with the stove
stops.date_confidence: attested date, disputed place: Wikipedia gives Neuburg an der Donau, the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy gives Ulm, and Descartes himself names no town
stops.campa: Winter shuts the roads and he takes a room warmed by a stove, alone, with no company that interests him and nothing he is required to do. He spends the whole day thinking. That night three dreams come one after another: a whirlwind that turns him against a chapel wall, a noise like a thunderclap, a book of poems falling open at the line quod vitae sectabor iter, what road in life shall I follow. He wakes certain they were sent, and certain of what they showed him, which was a single method for all the sciences. He wrote it down in a notebook that is lost. Baillet read it before it disappeared.
stops.quote: I was then in Germany, attracted thither by the wars in that country, which have not yet been brought to a termination; and as I was returning to the army from the coronation of the emperor, the setting in of winter arrested me in a locality where, as I found no society to interest me, and was besides fortunately undisturbed by any cares or passions, I remained the whole day in seclusion, with full opportunity to occupy my attention with my own thoughts.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part II, tr. John Veitch (1853); Veitch glosses the French as literally a room heated by means of a stove
suggested_refs: The lost Olympica notebook, summarized by Baillet in 1691
sources: Baillet, La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes (1691)
Descartes, Discourse on Method, Part Two

stops.name: Bílá Hora, near Prague: the hour that ended Bohemia
stops.date_confidence: attested date for the battle; his presence is reported, and whether he was on the field is disputed
stops.campa: The Bohemian revolt is finished in an hour on the slope of the White Mountain outside Prague, the Protestant army broken and the elected king in flight before dark. Descartes is with the imperial forces. One account has him there as an official observer, others put him with the baggage or riding up afterwards, and no line in his own hand places him on the field at all. He is twenty-four. The war he is riding with has twenty-eight years left to run.
suggested_refs: The battlefield and memorial cairn at Bílá hora, west of Prague
sources: Rodis-Lewis, who treats his presence as unverified

segments.name: Loreto, Rome, and the Selling of the Land

stops.name: Poitou, the inheritance turned into bonds
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the transactions are not itemized in the reachable sources
stops.campa: He comes back to Poitou and sells the farms and land that came to him through his mother, putting the proceeds into bonds. The income is modest, secure, and sufficient. What it purchases is the arrangement he will keep for the rest of his life: no patron, no post, no students, no order, no city that has any claim on him, and the means to move house the week a place stops suiting him. He is twenty-six. He will never hold a salaried position of any kind.
suggested_refs: The Poitou properties inherited from Jeanne Brochard and liquidated in 1622
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Loreto, the vow of the three dreams
stops.date_confidence: traditional; both the vow and the journey rest on Baillet alone
stops.campa: He crosses the Alps into Italy. Baillet has him walking to Loreto to discharge a vow made on the night of the three dreams, to the Holy House that angels are said to have carried out of Nazareth and set down above the Adriatic. That the vow was made at all rests on Baillet, and that the walk was finished rests on Baillet too. A man who will build a philosophy on accepting nothing he has not examined himself has promised a pilgrimage to a shrine. Did he arrive?
suggested_refs: The Basilica della Santa Casa at Loreto
sources: Baillet, La Vie de Monsieur Des-Cartes (1691)

stops.name: Rome, the Holy Year
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Italian years are the thinnest stretch of the documented life
stops.campa: Rome in the jubilee fills with pilgrims out of every Catholic country, and Descartes is among the travellers in it. He is nearly thirty. He has published nothing, holds no position, and has spent seven years on roads and in armies. What he writes afterwards about Italy concerns its manners rather than its monuments, and the difficulty of thinking clearly in that heat. The stretch between the Alps and his return to Paris is the worst documented part of his life. His biographers say so.
stops.quote: For to hold converse with those of other ages and to travel, are almost the same thing. It is useful to know something of the manners of different nations, that we may be enabled to form a more correct judgment regarding our own.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part I, tr. John Veitch (1853), Project Gutenberg e-text 59
suggested_refs: The 1625 Holy Year pilgrimage sites of Rome

stops.name: Paris, the circle around Mersenne
stops.date_confidence: attested for the period 1625-1628; the year given here is approximate within it
stops.campa: Back in Paris he falls in among the men who gather around Marin Mersenne, a Minim friar who keeps a correspondence with half the natural philosophers of Europe and moves their questions from one to another like a sorting office. Descartes works at optics, at the grinding of lenses, at the law that governs a ray bending as it enters water, and starts a treatise on method that he will abandon unfinished. For the next twenty years Mersenne handles his letters, his objectors and his printers, out of a friar's cell.
suggested_refs: The unfinished Rules for the Direction of the Mind, abandoned around 1628

stops.name: La Rochelle, the siege watched from outside
stops.date_confidence: contradiction not resolved: en.wikipedia and the chronology give 1627, the geographical dossier gives 1628; the siege itself ran from September 1627 to October 1628
stops.campa: The royal army has ringed the Huguenot port with earthworks and thrown a stone dyke across the harbour mouth to starve out the sea gate. Descartes goes to look at it. He is a Catholic gentleman among the besiegers and not a combatant, and this is the last of the wars of religion he watches from close up. Within a year he has wound up his affairs and left France for a republic his own church is formally at war with. Nobody there knows him. The printers are better and the rooms are cheap.
suggested_refs: Richelieu's dyke across the harbour mouth at La Rochelle
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Franeker, matriculated at the northern university
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1629 (SEP); the assumed-name detail belongs to Leiden the following year, not here
stops.campa: He registers at the small university of Franeker in Friesland, at the northern edge of the Republic, and is entered in the books as a student. He is thirty-three. What he wants is not the teaching but the arrangement that comes with it: rooms, a library, a legal standing, no duties, and a town where nobody has any occasion to call on him. Over the next twenty years he will change address more than twenty times inside this small country. Franeker is the first of them.
suggested_refs: The matriculation register of the University of Franeker, April 1629
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Amsterdam, the butchers and the treatise on light
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is approximate, and Amsterdam recurs as an address across two decades
stops.campa: In Amsterdam he takes lodgings and goes down to the butchers to watch animals opened, buying carcasses to dissect himself and following the vessels of the heart with his own hands. The city suits him exactly: crowded enough that a foreigner is nobody in particular, and stocked with printers, lens grinders, anatomists and ships to anywhere. Here he begins the treatise on light, weight, motion and the making of the world that he means to be the first thing he publishes.
suggested_refs: The Amsterdam lodgings of 1629-1630 and the dissections described in his correspondence

stops.name: Leiden, enrolled under the name Poitevin
stops.date_confidence: attested year for the Leiden matriculation under the name Poitevin; the month is approximate
stops.campa: He enrolls at Leiden University under the name Poitevin, after the province where his family land lay before he sold it. By now he is a known man in the Republic, writing to mathematicians in Paris and quarrelling with Beeckman over which of them had taught the other what. He signs on with a name that is his and is not. The assumed name and the unlisted address run right through the Dutch decades. Anyone who needed to reach him wrote to Mersenne in Paris.
suggested_refs: The Leiden matriculation of 1630 under the name Poitevin
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Deventer, writing Le Monde
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Deventer residence of 1632-1633
stops.campa: At Deventer he works on Le Monde, a physics with no room in it for the Aristotle he was taught at La Flèche: matter divided into particles, whirlpools of the stuff carrying planets round their stars, light as pressure travelling through a medium, and the earth in motion with the rest. He writes it as a fable about a world God might have made, which would happen to look precisely like this one. The device is transparent and he knows it is. By the autumn of 1633 the manuscript is close to finished.
suggested_refs: Le Monde, ou Traité de la lumière, written 1629-1633, published posthumously in 1664
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Deventer, the news of Galileo
stops.date_confidence: attested to late 1633, when word of the June condemnation reached the Republic; the month is approximate
stops.campa: Word reaches the Republic that the Roman Inquisition has made Galileo kneel and abjure, and that a book teaching the motion of the earth has been condemned in a Catholic court. Descartes writes to Mersenne that if the motion of the earth is false, then so are all the foundations of his own philosophy, and that he would rather burn the thing than publish anything the Church has condemned. He puts Le Monde away. It is printed fourteen years after his death, by other men.
suggested_refs: Descartes to Mersenne, late 1633, on the suppression of Le Monde

stops.name: Deventer, the birth of Francine
stops.date_confidence: attested year and town; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A daughter is born at Deventer to Helena Jans van der Strom, a servant in the house where he lodges, and is baptised Francine. The Deventer baptismal register names him as the father. He does not marry Helena and does not conceal the child either. Mother and daughter stay in his household and move with it. Nine years on, when he is back in France, he puts money toward a dowry so that Helena can marry. What he called the girl in company the letters do not say.
suggested_refs: The baptismal record of Francine at Deventer, 1635

stops.name: Leiden, Jan Maire prints the Discourse
stops.date_confidence: attested; the title page and the printing privilege fix the date
stops.campa: Jan Maire prints, with no author's name on it, a book in French instead of Latin: a discourse on the method of rightly conducting reason, with three essays behind it to show what the method can do. The Geometry fixes any curve by two numbered lines crossing at right angles. The Dioptrics gives the law of refraction. The Meteors takes apart the rainbow. Ninety-four years later a clerk of nineteen in the land registry at Chambéry works through Descartes, Locke and Voltaire in no order and with no teacher, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau can do that because the book was written in French.
stops.quote: I think, therefore I am (COGITO ERGO SUM), was so certain and of such evidence that no ground of doubt, however extravagant, could be alleged by the sceptics capable of shaking it.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part IV, tr. John Veitch (1853), Project Gutenberg e-text 59
suggested_refs: Discours de la méthode (Leiden: Jan Maire, 1637), first edition, published anonymously
sources: Title page of Discours de la méthode (Leiden: Jan Maire, 1637)

stops.name: The Dutch Republic, a daughter dead at five
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1640; the reachable sources do not name the town, and the coordinate here falls back on Deventer, where she was born
stops.campa: Francine takes scarlet fever and dies at five years old, in the autumn, in a town the surviving letters do not name. Those who knew him report that he wept, and that he called it the greatest sorrow of his life. He is at that moment finishing a book which argues that the soul is a thinking thing wholly distinct from the body, more easily known than the body, and not touched by anything that happens to bodies. The manuscript goes to the printer the following spring.
stops.quote: So that 'I,' that is to say, the mind by which I am what I am, is wholly distinct from the body, and is even more easily known than the latter.
stops.quote_source: Discourse on the Method, Part IV, tr. John Veitch (1853), Project Gutenberg e-text 59
suggested_refs: The letters of autumn 1640 reporting Francine's death

stops.name: Endegeest, the moated castle outside Leiden
stops.date_confidence: attested: fr.wikipedia gives 31 March 1641 for the move, nl.wikipedia the residence 1641-1643; the dossier's 1637 start date was wrong
stops.campa: On the last day of March he moves into a small moated castle at Oegstgeest outside Leiden, with a garden, a farm attached and a short road to the university. It is the grandest address he ever keeps and he keeps it for two years. The Meditations are written by then and going round in manuscript among the objectors Mersenne has recruited for him; what he does at Endegeest is answer them in writing, one theologian and one mathematician at a time, and have the answers bound into his own book.
suggested_refs: Kasteel Endegeest, Oegstgeest, occupied by Descartes 1641-1643
sources: Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Paris, the Meditations printed with their objections
stops.date_confidence: attested year of first publication in Paris; the month is approximate, and the second Amsterdam edition follows in 1642
stops.campa: The Meditations on First Philosophy is printed in Latin with six sets of objections and his replies bound in behind it: Hobbes, Gassendi, Arnauld, the Jesuits, and Mersenne's own gathered from anyone he could reach. The book opens by pulling down everything its author believes, the evidence of his senses included, and the certainty that he is even awake, then rebuilds from the single thing left standing. In 1966, at the height of his Paris fame, Michel Foucault is teaching in Tunis and lecturing on this book to students who arrive from political meetings.
stops.quote: I was convinced of the necessity of undertaking once in my life to rid myself of all the opinions I had adopted, and of commencing anew the work of building from the foundation.
stops.quote_source: Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation I, English translation, Wikisource
suggested_refs: Meditationes de prima philosophia (Paris, 1641), with the six sets of Objections and Replies

stops.name: Utrecht, the charge of atheism
stops.date_confidence: attested: Voetius attacks from 1639, the academic senate condemns the new philosophy in March 1642, the appeal to the French ambassador follows in 1643; the dossier's 1635 start date was too early
stops.campa: Gisbertus Voetius, rector at Utrecht and the hardest Calvinist in the Republic, has been going after the new philosophy from pulpit and chair since 1639. In March the academic senate condemns it. The charge laid is atheism, which at Utrecht is not an academic matter but one for the magistrates, and the city moves toward proceedings against him. Descartes writes pamphlets, loses his temper in print, and finally asks the French ambassador and the Prince of Orange to keep him out of a municipal court. He had crossed the border to get away from precisely this.
suggested_refs: The Utrecht senate's condemnation of the new philosophy, March 1642, and the ensuing pamphlet war with Voetius

stops.name: The Hague, the first letter from Elisabeth
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated
stops.campa: Elisabeth of Bohemia is twenty-four, granddaughter of James I, living with her exiled family at The Hague after the war that drove them out of Bohemia while Descartes was riding with the other side of it. She has read the Meditations closely. Her first letter puts to him the question the book does not answer: if the soul is nothing but a thinking thing, how does it get an arm to move. He answers her, and goes on answering until the year before his own death.
stops.quote: Given that the soul of a human being is only a thinking substance, how can it affect the bodily spirits, in order to bring about voluntary actions?
stops.quote_source: Princess Elisabeth to Descartes, 6 May 1643, tr. Jonathan Bennett, earlymoderntexts.com (2017 ed.), which modernizes forms of address
suggested_refs: The Descartes-Elisabeth correspondence, 1643-1649, in Adam and Tannery, Oeuvres de Descartes
sources: Correspondence between Descartes and Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, tr. Bennett

stops.name: The Hague, what a princess has to spend her day on
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated
stops.campa: She writes again in June and apologises for the delay. The interests of her house, which she may not neglect, and the conversations and social obligations she cannot get out of, leave her mind useless for anything else for a long while afterwards. Then she goes back to the argument and presses him on whether an unextended thing can act on a body at all, or whether he has quietly given the soul extension after all. She holds onto that objection for years. His other critics let it go after a letter or two.
stops.quote: The interests of my house (which I must not neglect) and conversations and social obligations (which I can't avoid), inflict so much annoyance and boredom on this weak mind of mine that it is useless for anything else for a long time afterward.
stops.quote_source: Princess Elisabeth to Descartes, 10 June 1643, tr. Jonathan Bennett, earlymoderntexts.com (2017 ed.)
suggested_refs: Elisabeth's letters of May and June 1643, the opening of the mind-body correspondence
sources: Correspondence between Descartes and Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, tr. Bennett

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Principles of Philosophy
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is approximate
stops.campa: The Principles of Philosophy comes out in Latin, dedicated to Elisabeth: metaphysics in the first part, then matter, motion, the vortices, the planets, magnets and the earth, laid out in numbered articles like a scholastic textbook so that it could be set in front of students in place of Aristotle. In 1723 Leonhard Euler takes his master's degree at Basel with a dissertation setting Descartes's natural philosophy against Newton's, and in 1746 Immanuel Kant's first manuscript takes up the quarrel between the Cartesians and the Leibnizians over how force is to be measured.
suggested_refs: Principia philosophiae (Amsterdam, 1644), dedicated to Elisabeth of Bohemia

stops.name: Egmond-Binnen, vulgar souls and great souls
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated and written from Egmond
stops.campa: He has settled in the country near Egmond, with a garden he keeps and animals he cuts up for his physiology, and this becomes the longest single address of his Dutch years. Elisabeth has been unwell and low, and he writes to her about the passions: that vulgar souls hand themselves over to whatever happens to them, and that great souls reason so powerfully that even afflictions are made to serve them. The letters go on for four more years. Out of them comes his last book.
stops.quote: Vulgar souls give themselves over to their passions and are happy or sad purely according to whether what happens to them is agreeable or unpleasant; whereas great souls reason so powerfully that... their reason remains in command and brings it about that even afflictions serve them and contribute to the perfect happiness that they can enjoy already in this life.
stops.quote_source: Descartes to Princess Elisabeth, 18 May 1645, written from Egmond, tr. Jonathan Bennett, earlymoderntexts.com (2017 ed.); the ellipsis marks a short omitted clause
suggested_refs: The Egmond-Binnen country house, his longest Dutch residence
sources: Correspondence between Descartes and Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, tr. Bennett
Rodis-Lewis, Descartes: His Life and Thought (1995)

stops.name: Paris, the Principles in French
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: A French translation of the Principles is published at Paris, ten years after the Discourse first put his method into the vernacular. The system he could not print in 1633 is now on sale in Paris in a language anyone can read, complete, dedicated to a princess, and disreputable enough back in the Republic that the professors who teach it there are being disciplined for it. Everything he means to publish is in print now except for one book. He is fifty-one years old.
suggested_refs: Les Principes de la philosophie (Paris, 1647), the French Principles

stops.name: Amsterdam, the broadsheet against Regius
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Henricus Regius, the Utrecht physician who taught Cartesian medicine before anyone else dared and whom Descartes once counted a disciple, has published a broadsheet arguing that the mind may be a mode of the body rather than a substance in its own right. Descartes answers in print, coldly, article by article, and disowns him. Almost every quarrel of his Dutch years takes this shape. The Aristotelians mostly ignore him. The trouble comes from the men who take up his physics and leave the soul behind.
suggested_refs: Notae in programma quoddam (Comments on a Certain Broadsheet), Amsterdam, 1648

stops.name: Egmond-Binnen, one foot in each country
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated only to June or July 1648 in Bennett's edition
stops.campa: He has been down to France and come back again, as he has done every few years since 1628, and each return to Holland is a decision rather than a habit. He owns no house. He holds no post, belongs to no faculty and no order, answers to no city. Thirty years of arranging have gone into making sure no institution anywhere has a hold on him. He is fifty-two. From Egmond he writes to Elisabeth that, having one foot in each country, he finds his condition a very happy one in that it is free.
stops.quote: Meanwhile, having one foot in each country, I find my condition a very happy one in that it is free.
stops.quote_source: Descartes to Elisabeth, June or July 1648, tr. Jonathan Bennett, earlymoderntexts.com, descartes1643_4.pdf, p. 64; the wording circulating on Wikiquote could not be traced to any source and is not used here
suggested_refs: The 1648 letters to Elisabeth in Bennett's translation of the correspondence
sources: Correspondence between Descartes and Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia, tr. Bennett

stops.name: Amsterdam, The Passions of the Soul
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the month is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: The Passions of the Soul is printed in French, the last book he publishes: an anatomy of wonder, love, hatred, desire, joy and sadness, treated as motions of the blood and the animal spirits which a mind can be trained to govern. It came out of six years of letters to Elisabeth about grief, illness and how to be well when circumstances are not. The question she asked him in 1643 is answered here in plumbing, with a small gland at the centre of the brain doing the work of joining the two substances.
suggested_refs: Les Passions de l'âme (Amsterdam, 1649), his last published book

stops.name: Amsterdam harbour, the ship for Stockholm
stops.date_confidence: attested to the autumn of 1649; the sailing date is approximate
stops.campa: Christina of Sweden has asked twice, and he goes. He is unwilling and says so to his friends: he is going to the land of bears, between rock and ice, and he settles his papers before leaving in the manner of a man not certain of the return trip. Twenty-one years in the Republic are behind him, more than twenty addresses in it, and every book he wrote there is in print. A reigning monarch wanting lessons is the one summons he has never had before. He is fifty-three years old and has never in his life got up early.
suggested_refs: Descartes's letters of 1649 on the summons to Sweden, in Adam and Tannery
sources: Descartes's letters of 1649, in Adam and Tannery, Oeuvres de Descartes

stops.name: Stockholm, Tre Kronor: five o'clock in the morning
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1649-1650; the specific starting date of the lessons is not documented in the reachable sources
stops.campa: The queen is twenty-two, reads Greek, and has decided to take her philosophy at five in the morning, before the day's business, in a library across the courtyard, in a Swedish December. Descartes has risen late every morning since the Jesuits let a sickly boy stay in bed at La Flèche, and has been telling correspondents for thirty years that the hours in bed are the hours he thinks in. He crosses the palace yard in the dark, several mornings a week, through the coldest winter anyone there can remember.
suggested_refs: The Tre Kronor palace at Stockholm, destroyed by fire in 1697
sources: Descartes's correspondence with Constantijn Huygens on his late mornings

stops.name: Stockholm, the house of the ambassador Chanut
stops.date_confidence: attested; the death date is fixed by Chanut's own dispatches
stops.campa: He lodges with Pierre Chanut, the French ambassador, and it is there that he takes to his bed at the beginning of February with fever and an inflammation of the lungs. He refuses treatment from the queen's physician, a Dutchman named van Wullen whom he does not trust. Chanut calls the illness peripneumonia in his report. He dies on the eleventh of February, seven weeks short of fifty-four. A theory that he was poisoned with arsenic has been raised more than once since and has never been settled either way.
suggested_refs: Chanut's dispatches reporting the death, February 1650, in Adam and Tannery
sources: Chanut's letters, 1650, in Adam and Tannery, Oeuvres de Descartes
Rodis-Lewis, who leaves the poisoning question unresolved

stops.name: Stockholm, the ground kept for foreigners and unbaptised children
stops.date_confidence: the burial date is given as 14 February in the dossier but could not be corroborated in any reachable source; the funeral is usually placed later in February
stops.campa: A Catholic cannot be laid in consecrated Lutheran ground. He is buried instead in a small plot outside the walls kept for foreigners and for children who died before baptism, in a corner by the wall, the ambassador's household attending. The chapel that stood there then was St Olof's. A century and more later a new parish church, Adolf Fredriks kyrka, is built over the same ground, and Gustav III installs a memorial to him inside it. The body had been dug up and carried off to France long before the memorial went up.
suggested_refs: Adolf Fredriks kyrka, Stockholm, built 1768-1774 over the older burial ground

stops.name: Paris, the abbey church of Sainte-Geneviève
stops.date_confidence: attested by fr.wikipedia: exhumed 1 May 1666, in Paris January 1667, interred 24 June 1667; English accounts frequently give the wrong church
stops.campa: His bones are lifted in Stockholm on the first of May 1666 and sealed into a copper box. The box reaches Paris in January 1667, waits a while at the church of Saint-Paul, and on the twenty-fourth of June is placed in the abbey church of Sainte-Geneviève on the hill above the university, with a marble monument added two years later. English accounts routinely name the neighbouring parish church, Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, instead. The abbey church itself was pulled down in 1804 and a street laid across the ground.
suggested_refs: The site of the abbey church of Sainte-Geneviève, now the Lycée Henri-IV, where only the old bell tower survives

stops.name: Paris, the teaching of his philosophy forbidden
stops.date_confidence: attested years: the Index in 1663 under Alexander VII, the royal prohibition in 1671; the month of the 1671 order is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Alexander VII puts his works on the Index in 1663, and in 1671 Louis XIV forbids the teaching of his philosophy in the schools and universities of France. Neither prohibition does what prohibitions are for. At Trinity College in 1664 Isaac Barrow is remembered as examining a young Isaac Newton and finding him weak on Euclid and strong on Descartes, though that story reaches us only through Conduitt, half a century after the fact. At Naples in 1708 Giambattista Vico opens the academic year with an oration against the reigning Cartesian fashion.
suggested_refs: The 1663 Index decree and the 1671 royal prohibition on teaching Cartesian philosophy in France

stops.name: Paris, the Panthéon decree that was never carried out
stops.date_confidence: attested: Marie-Joseph Chénier's motion of 2 October 1793; en.wikipedia's 1792 is wrong, the Convention had only convened on 21 September 1792
stops.campa: On the second of October 1793 Marie-Joseph Chénier proposes to the National Convention that the remains of Descartes be carried into the Panthéon among the great men of the nation. The Convention decrees it. Nothing whatever is done. The Revolution wants him for an ancestor, a Frenchman who threw out every authority and began again from what one mind could establish for itself sitting alone in a warm room. Eleven years later the abbey church holding him is demolished. His name is inscribed in the Panthéon; his remains have never entered it.
suggested_refs: Chénier's motion of 2 October 1793 and the unexecuted Convention decree

stops.name: Saint-Germain-des-Prés, the reburial without a head
stops.date_confidence: attested to 26 February 1819 (fr.wikipedia)
stops.campa: On the twenty-sixth of February 1819 what remains of him is reburied in the abbey church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where a slab in the floor names him and where he lies today. The men who opened the coffin found the skeleton short of one finger and short of its skull. The head and the body have been in separate custody since the exhumation of 1666 and have never been brought back together. Whether anyone at the 1819 ceremony said so out loud is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The floor slab naming Descartes in the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés

stops.name: Musée de l'Homme, the skull with the writing on it
stops.date_confidence: attested: brought to France by Berzelius in 1821, held at the Jardin des Plantes, transferred to the Musée de l'Homme collections in 1931; the dossier's 1878 was wrong in both directions
stops.campa: A skull with a chain of owners' names inked across the cranium comes up at auction in Sweden, is bought by the chemist Berzelius, carried to France in 1821, handed to Georges Cuvier, and put into the anatomical collection at the Jardin des Plantes; in 1931 it passes to the Musée de l'Homme, a few miles across the river from the rest of the skeleton. The inscriptions trace it back to a Swedish officer at the 1666 exhumation. Five other skulls have at one time or another been claimed as his.
suggested_refs: The inscribed cranium held by the Musée de l'Homme, Paris

stops.name: Descartes, Indre-et-Loire: the town takes the name
stops.date_confidence: attested: renamed during the Revolution, La Haye-Descartes from 1802, and simply Descartes from 1967 after the merger with Balesmes
stops.campa: La Haye takes his name during the Revolution, becomes La Haye-Descartes in 1802, and in 1967, after merging with the neighbouring commune, drops everything but Descartes. The house he was born in is a museum. A statue of him stands near the town hall. At La Flèche, where he actually spent eight years, no monument to him survives on the campus at all. He left the Touraine at eleven and never lived there again. The road signs on every approach to the town carry his name.
suggested_refs: The Musée Descartes in the maison natale, and the statue near the town hall of Descartes, Indre-et-Loire
